essay_student_00_glm.text:
On April 3rd 1948, President Truman signed into law the European Recovery Program, now popularly called the Marshall Plan. The future of West Germany, destroyed in its industrial cities, the currency almost valueless, the economy still circumscribed by Allied occupation control measures (steel output limited; industrial plants broken up) did not look too bright. But within the next 4 years, some $1.4 billion from the Marshall Plan went to the future Federal Republic of Germany, and played a large part in what proved one of the most successful economic recoveries of the 20th century.

Marshall Plan assistance to West Germany, administered through the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), was not so much impressive in the quantity of goods (cotton, wheat, coal, machinery) sent over (paid for in almost valueless Reichsmarks, and the money steered towards a special counterpart fund). But it was important in its timing and role. West Germany was supplied with goods. The special counterpart fund was many billion DM in size and later used to invest in new infrastructure and industry. This helped finance the upgrading of electrical networks, and the growth of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley for example. The Marshall Plan money also took care of Germany's perpetual trade deficit in 1949 and 1950. This gave the new West German state time to see its currency reforms of June 1948 (bringing in the Deutschmark) take effect.

The Marshall Plan also had an important institutional impact. One condition of accepting US help was membership in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This brought West Germany into a European co-operation framework which would later lead to the formation in the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. Second, under US pressure, controls by the occupying forces were eased. Steel production limits went up gradually, from c. 5.8 million tons to over 11 million in the early 1950s, and there was less dismantling of industrial plants. And a newly appointed (1948) Economic Director, economist Ludwig Erhard combined the new opportunities with his "social market economy" principle: free market competition with social safety net.

West German industrial output soared in 1948-52, about doubled. And by mid-1950s, West Germany was producing more than before the war. The government of Konrad Adenauer's, Chancellor, called this "economic miracle," or Wirtschaftswunder. As historians are careful to point out that there were many other factors, besides Marshall Plan, that led to this (currency reforms; demand due to Korean War; skilled labor, etc.). But it is true that the US help did not merely repair the West German economy. It changed it. Changed it Europe-wards, trade-wards, changed it towards a stable democratic capitalism, which became the hallmark of the Federal Republic for many years to come.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the European Recovery Program, more commonly known as the Marshall Plan. The prospects for economic development in West Germany appeared at the time to be very limited: industrial centers in ruins, a practically valueless currency, and limitations on economic activity because of Allied occupation measures that had limited steel production and dismantled industrial facilities. In the following four years, about $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan assistance was introduced into what would later be the Federal Republic of Germany and helped kickstart one of the most spectacular economic recoveries of the 20th century.

Marshall Plan aid, administered by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), was important, not so much because of its scale, but because of its timing and purpose. The Marshall Plan brought in goods for West Germany to use, such as cotton, wheat, coal, or machinery, which it paid for in nearly worthless Reichsmark. The money from these goods was placed in a so-called counterpart fund. This fund, worth several billion Deutschmarks, was later invested in infrastructure development or industry. Thus, for example, modernization of electrical grids or development of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley could be partially financed. At the same time, Marshall Plan funds were used to pay off Germany's permanent trade deficit in 1949 and 1950, thus buying time for the newly established West German state to stabilize its economy with the currency reform in June 1948 (the introduction of the Deutschmark).

The Marshall Plan helped effect important structural changes. First, the acceptance of US aid made it necessary to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This led West Germany into the sphere of European cooperation, which would later culminate in the European Coal and Steel Community of 1951. Second, through American pressure, limits on German economic activity were gradually loosened. The limit on steel production was successively raised from about 5.8 to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. The dismantling of industrial facilities was essentially stopped. The new Economic Director, Ludwig Erhard, installed in 1948, used these new opportunities to implement his “social market economy.” Under it, he combined elements of competition in the free market with a system of social security.

The consequences were phenomenal. West German industrial production almost doubled from 1948 to 1952. In the mid-1950s, West Germany was producing more than it did before the war. The Konrad Adenauer government hailed this as the so-called “economic miracle” or Wirtschaftswunder. Of course, as historians point out, the Marshall Plan is only one factor among many that led to the revival. Other key factors include the currency reform, demand related to the Korean War, or the highly qualified workforce. It can be said, however, that US aid for West Germany did not just help to reconstruct its economy, but also to reshape it, namely in the direction of Europe, towards trade, and towards a stable democratic form of capitalism, which would characterize the Federal Republic for many years to come.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the European Recovery Program (more popularly known as the Marshall Plan) into law. The prospects for West Germany's economy at that point were dire. Its industrial cities were gutted, its currency near worthless. Its economy was still bound by the controls of Allied occupation forces which had limited steel output and de-installed industrial facilities. Over the next four years, however, the Federal Republic of Germany would receive about $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan assistance, which would help set the stage for one of the most spectacular economic turn-arounds of the 20th century.

The Marshall Plan assistance, delivered via the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), was less a question of the amounts given than when and how they were given. West Germany received goods in the form of cotton, wheat, coal, and machinery, paid for in nearly worthless Reichsmarks, and the income from that went into a special counterpart fund. This several billion Deutschmark counterpart fund would eventually be re-invested in West Germany's infrastructure and industry, and, as such, helped fund improvements in electrical networks and increased production in the steel industry of the Ruhr Valley, for instance. Just as critical was the fact that the Marshall Plan assistance provided funding for the chronic West German trade deficit in 1949 and 1950. This gave the young West German state time for its own June 1948 currency reform (creating the Deutschmark) to have an effect.

In another critical way, the Marshall Plan was also the impetus for important changes in institutional structures. In order to receive American assistance, a nation had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This meant West Germany's incorporation into a European cooperative network that would eventually lead to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. Also, with the pressure from the Americans, the West German economy began to see the relaxation of restrictions, such as the increasing of limits on steel production (from roughly 5.8 to over 11 million tons in the early 1950s) and the halting of further de-installation of facilities. This, along with Ludwig Erhard's "social market economy" policy, which he implemented as the new Economic Director in 1948 (a combination of free-market competition and a social safety net), allowed for further expansion.

And expansion there was. West Germany's industrial output rose about two-fold from 1948-1952. By the mid-1950s, it was putting out more than before the war, which the government of Chancellor Konrad Adenauer heralded as the Wirtschaftswunder, or "economic miracle." The Marshall Plan was only one factor in this, of course. There were many others, such as the currency reform, Korean War demand, and a qualified labor force. So historians are right to point out. But it's not too much to say that the Marshall Plan did not just revive West Germany's economy. It also transformed it, making it more European, more of a trading economy, and one that formed the basis for stable, democratic capitalism, which would characterize the Federal Republic for decades to come.

After the enactment of the European Recovery Program (the Marshall Plan) by President Truman on April 3, 1948, the economic prospects for West Germany seemed grim. The industrial cities were devastated and the currency was almost worthless. The Allied occupation program's steel production quota and industrial plant dismantling policies continued to stifle the economy. However, during the next 4 years some $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan assistance poured into the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) and served to help trigger one of the great economic resurrections of the 20th century.

The sheer volume of Marshall Plan assistance provided via the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) was not so important as the nature, timing and use. West Germany received goods, including cotton, wheat, coal and machinery, which could be paid for in near-worthless Reichsmarks. These payments were pooled into a special 'counterpart' fund. This fund of several billion Deutschmarks would subsequently be re-invested in such infrastructure and industrial development as the upgrading of electrical grids and the expansion of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley. Equally critical was Marshall Plan assistance's ability to bridge the trade deficit of West Germany in 1949 and 1950. This gave West Germany's fledgling government some valuable time in which its currency reform of June 1948 (which resulted in the introduction of the Deutschmark) could take effect.

The Marshall Plan itself required some vital institutional changes. In order to accept Marshall Plan aid, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC). This drew West Germany into a structure of European cooperation which would eventually lead to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. Also, American pressure eased the occupation program constraints. Steel production quotas were gradually increased from about 5.8 to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s. The dismantling of industrial plants was largely discontinued. In 1948, the Economic Director Ludwig Erhard used this newly gained latitude to implement his 'social market economy' policy which stressed the combination of free-market competition with a social welfare system.

West Germany's industrial output increased approximately two-fold from 1948-1952. By the mid 1950s West Germany was producing more goods than it had produced pre-war. This 'economic miracle' or Wirtschaftswunder was noted by Chancellor Konrad Adenauer and his government. As historians point out, the Marshall Plan played only a part among many factors. Currency reform, demand for goods in Korea, the availability of a skilled labor force, also contributed to the success. However, it is legitimate to say that American assistance not only rebuilt West Germany's economy. It redirected West Germany's economy. It redirected it toward Europe. It redirected it toward commerce. It redirected West Germany toward a stable capitalist democracy that would last for decades within the Federal Republic.

Harriet Tubman was making 13 (approx) journeys in and out of the slaveholder's South between 1849 and (somewhere around) 1860. Every trip was a direct challenge to federal law. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 was enacted, it was now not just a crime to escape slavery, but also to aid and abet the escape of others. Fines of up to $1,000 and imprisonment were the consequences for abettors. Jury trial was denied to alleged fugitives. Ordinary citizens in the North were required to help with fugitives on demand. For Harriet Tubman, who fled slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in 1849, the response was to re-enter the very place where this Act was meant to exert control. 
 Harriet's solution was to manipulate the Fugitive Slave Act to her advantage. Moving people north in the dark (frequently during winter when patrols were lighter and the night longer) while following the North Star, and utilizing networks of word-of-mouth contacts (the Underground Railroad). After 1850, with the impact of the new Act's reach into free states, Tubman would even widen her route to St. Catharines, Ontario in Canada, where British law would further protect escaped persons from US marshals. According to estimates, Tubman guided 70 (herself, family, etc) escaped persons to freedom. All of this against a background of what was allegedly a $40,000 bounty on her head for capture. 
 Harriet's missions were a direct challenge to the Fugitive Slave Act (not just her own escapes), because she kept coming back in. Under the Act, the fear factor was the one way border lock. Tubman crossed repeatedly in the most dangerous direction to aid others in escaping. Tubman was armed with a pistol for her own defense. But also, according to reports later on, to push forward any hesitating member of the group threatening to return and risk exposure. During the Civil War period, Tubman challenged federal law by further serving as scout and spy for the Union Army. Helping lead the 1863 Combahee River raid in South Carolina freed over 700 persons from slavery in one night. 
 The 13 missions of Harriet Tubman demonstrate that the Fugitive Slave Act, so severe on its face, was no match for a person willing to consider the penalties the Act provides a cost of doing business, rather than a deterrent.

From 1849 to around 1860, Harriet Tubman undertook somewhere around 13 trips back into slave holding territory. All of them illegal under federal law. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 not only made it illegal for people to escape slavery. It also made it illegal to help them. It also introduced up to $1,000 fines and prison sentences for abettors. It also denied a jury trial to alleged fugitives and required that every day people in the North help at the drop of a hat with captures. Baking (or more specifically, using an oven toaster/air fryer) will always win over microwave.  Microwave makes crust turn into rubbery cardboard - it just warms up the internal moisture that's held in the breading. 
 1) Let your chicken sit out and get to room temperature first (20-30min).  Cold -> hot straight from fridge will not heat up evenly and you'll overcook the outside to warm up the middle.
 2) Preheat oven to 400°F (200C).  Make sure to put a wire rack inside of a sheet pan.  This is the most important step people often forget to do.  The air circulation below will prevent the bottom from steaming/getting soggy (which will happen if you just put it on top of sheet pan directly).
 3) Bake it for 15-20min if it's bone-in and 10-12min if it's boneless/tenders.  Flip once in the middle.  Your goal is to get internal temp to 165°F (74C).  Use instant read thermometer in the thickest part closest to the bone.
 4) Don't cover it in foil or anything.  You want to avoid trapping steam which will make the step 2 ineffective. 
 If you have an air fryer, this can even be faster/maybe even crispier.  Set it to 375°F (190C) and cook it for 4-6min.  No need to flip it as it will be air circulation from all angles.  I've done this with leftover KFC style thighs and popeyes tenders.  They were almost as crispy as fresh. 
 If the breading still feels slightly soft after reheating, you can broil it in the last 60-90seconds or so.  Watch it closely so it doesn't burn.  This will give it direct heat blast to crisp up the parts convection missed. 
 Don't ever use microwave unless you don't give a fuck about crust.  Even 30 seconds will have noticeable difference.

The solution is not to use Git merge resolution. It's to avoid multiple people editing the same lines often.

In our checkout-web repo, Maya is the owner of the layout of CartSummary.jsx. Jordan is the owner of the tax calc hook. We break it into smaller files.

```text
CartSummary/
  CartSummary.jsx
  useCartTotals.js
  CartLineItem.jsx
  CartSummary.test.jsx
```

We each work on a temporary branch (maya/cart-layout or jordan/tax-hook). We branch directly from main right before we work on it. We don't hold the branch for weeks, we do the pull request in 1-2 days. We run this before making a pull request

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
npm test -- CartSummary
```

And also try to pass data to the component via props instead of multiple people editing internal logic. E.g. you could have CartSummary.jsx be the JSX that renders subtotal, tax, total and you have useCartTotals.js that does the calculation. Then Jordan can change calculations without affecting Maya's JSX.

When there absolutely needs to be two changes that affect the same lines, decide the order in which you're going to integrate. Let's say on 9/21/2026 Maya does a structural refactor. Then you want to do it first so Maya's refactor can be merged first. Then Jordan can rebase on it and change the interface of the hook. You don't want to do the conflict resolution on your own in each branch.

And keep your commits small & focused. It's much easier to review & rebase a commit that's called "Extract CartLineItem" than a commit that has formatting changes, dependency upgrades, and business logic in it. Have branch protection on and require a successful CI check. That way when you make the second PR, it's tested against whatever the current main is before it merges.

So the best solution is not to rely on Git conflict resolution but make sure to have the least possible amount of overlaps in code edits done by different people.

For instance in our checkout-web repo we have Maya doing the CartSummary.jsx layout and Jordan doing the tax calculation hook. We separate the component into different files.

CartSummary/
 CartSummary.jsx
 useCartTotals.js
 CartLineItem.jsx
 CartSummary.test.jsx

Each person creates a short-lived branch, e.g. maya/cart-layout, jordan/tax-hook. Branch from main right before you start working on the changes. We PR withing 1-2 days rather than have these branches live for weeks. And before we PR we do:

git fetch origin
 git rebase origin/main
 npm test -- CartSummary

We also want to try and pass down data via props to the component rather than having multiple devs messing with the same internal logic. Not usually, and this catches a lot of people off guard as things changed in 2018. 
 If you are a W-2 employee (which "working remotely for my employer" suggests) then the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act suspended the miscellaneous itemized deduction for unreimbursed employee business expenses (which includes home office deduction) through 2025 (2018 through 2025 tax years). So whether you work 1 day/week from home, 5 days/week, as a W-2 employee, you are just not allowed to take the home office deduction on your federal return. Period.  Even if your employer mandates this hybrid schedule and you don't have a permanent office on the in-office days. 
 Variables that could alter things: 
 1. Are you a 1099 contractor or have self-employment income? If any of your income is from self employment, like some side gig freelance consulting from your home office, then you can take a business use deduction for your home for that income (Form 8829). You still need to meet "regular and exclusive use" though, so if you have a home office that is also a guest room on the weekends, then doesn't count. 
 2. State taxes. For a few states, California, NY, PA, Alabama, Arkansas you can still take the unreimbursed employee expense deduction on state returns even though it's suspended for federal taxes. Confirm for your state for 2025 rules. 
 3. Your employer does not reimburse you. See if your employer has an "accountable plan". If they are reimbursing you for a portion of your internet, a monitor etc. in an "accountable plan" then that is not taxable income to you, so that is actually better than a deduction in many ways. 
 So for a typical hybrid W-2 employee situation. No home office deduction on the federal side. See your state, see if your employer will reimburse you directly for the expenses. 
 Not tax advice specific to your situation, have a CPA confirm based on your complete return.

Do you have 3-6 months emergency fund. No credit card debt? If so, I'd squeeze every employer 401k match I can. Then... Are your student loans possibly forgivable?

If you are at a qualifying non profit/government employer check to see if you are PSLF eligible before paying anything extra. Like if you have 42k in federal Direct loans and you believe you can get to 120 qualifying payments... I'd typically argue for making necessary income driven payments. And investing your excess vs. voluntarily paying down something that may be forgivable. Since studentaid.gov is clear that qualifying payments/employment is a factor... Dont assume forgivable without checking your account and employer.

If it's not realistic to think they are forgivable... I'd probably do a hybrid. Enough to the Roth IRA to develop the habit (say $3750 in 2026). Rest to 6.8% loan. 6.8% guaranteed return by paying down the loan. Vs. potentially making more/less over decades on the Roth IRA investments. 6.8%... it's not "cheap" debt.

Plus opportunity cost. 2026 IRA max is $7500 for <50 yrs old. Once the 2026 contribution window passes... You generally can't get it back. You can put extra towards a loan next year. But you can't go back and make 2026 Roth space that wasn't used. Meaning you should at least fund the Roth in 2026 (if you qualify on income).

For someone with 30k remaining. Steady job. No forgivable path. 30 years until retirement. I'd probably fund the Roth. But make required payments on the loan. If debt free is a huge priority or your emergency fund is not great... I'd give the loan more priority. After getting the employer match.

If you have 3-6 month emergency fund saved and no credit card debt... I would personally prioritize 100% of available 401k (employer match) from your employer, and then... If there's a chance for student loan forgiveness... it will depend on that. 
 If you work for eligible employer (non-profit/gov) and are eligible for PSLF.... check first if you are eligible for PSLF before making any extra payments. Example, if you have $42,000 Federal Direct Loans and you are about to hit 120 eligible payments... probably best to just make required payments on income driven repayment and put the rest of the money to use elsewhere vs over paying off the loan to potentially be forgiven later. Make sure you check account/employer because studentaid.gov does mention you need to make qualifying payments + qualify on employment.  

 If no chance for forgiveness.... I'm probably going to do both... enough to Roth IRA to maintain a habit (say in 2026 you may want to put $3,750 there). And then put the rest towards your 6.8% loan. You'll get 6.8% guaranteed return by paying it down. Your investments in Roth IRA... it may grow more in decades but then it could also lose money as well. It's not "cheap" debt if it's at 6.8%. 
 Also... you need to consider an opportunity cost. If we're talking about 2026... you only get $7,500 Roth IRA under 50... so once your opportunity to make contribution in 2026 is gone... you most likely can't "get it back". Sure... you can make extra payments on loan next year... but you can't "go back" and make non-used space for 2026 in Roth. 
 So that tells me... at least make Roth happen in 2026 as long as you are eligible based on income. 
 With $30,000 remaining, and secured employment, and not eligible for forgiveness and 30 years before you're able to retire... I would probably lean towards making the Roth work and make all required payments on the loan. If getting out of debt is your big goal and/or you don't have a strong emergency fund... priority would be to pay loan after taking employer match.

Intense and ambitious, Christopher Nolan's 2023 film Oppenheimer works especially well in IMAX. The sheer scale of the IMAX format really immerses you in the Trinity test scene. The quiet before the blast, the flash of light, the delayed sound, it's like an ominous sense of dread and not just spectacle. Ludwig Goransson's score and the pounding sound effects support this without feeling like an action film. 
 Cillian Murphy is magnificent as J. Robert Oppenheimer. He comes across as both brilliant, vain, anxious, and increasingly consumed by the ramifications of his work. A tremendous cast supports him well too. Especially Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss. Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer. Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves. The time hops and B&W segments can be confusing at first, but it slowly forms a fascinating look at how science started to get wrapped up in politics, ego, and fear. 
 Oppenheimer is a long film at 3 hours. It does drag in some courtroom/security hearing scenes. There is a lot of dialogue to digest and you need to pay attention. But most of the time the length makes sense. You're getting the whole story of the Manhattan project. Of Oppenheimer's personal life. The political aftermath over a span of decades. The scale and detail in IMAX makes it easier to swallow (though I'd recommend taking a bathroom break beforehand). It's not a relaxing historical piece, it's an engrossing and draining film. That you'll think about long after it's over.

Oppenheimer (2023) is an ambitious, intense film. Particularly striking to see in IMAX. The large screen is perfect for making the Trinity sequence of Oppenheimer incredibly impactful. From the quiet build up of tension before the explosion, the sudden bright flash, and the delayed thunder you can really feel the mounting terror. The soundtrack from Ludwig Göransson and the hard hitting sound design in the film support everything without falling into action film territory. 
 The cast are excellent, with Cillian Murphy giving a great performance as J. Robert Oppenheimer. Making the character charming but self-absorbed, and nervous and tortured by the repercussions of his work. Especially excellent are Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss, Emily Blunt as Kitty Oppenheimer, and Matt Damon as General Leslie Groves. It's a bit disorienting at first with the jumping timelines and the black and white bits, but it starts to really come together and paint an interesting picture of how science and achievement had mixed with politics, ego, and fear. 
 It's certainly a long movie at 3 hours. Some of the courtroom or security hearing scenes do drag a bit, and you really need to listen hard as it's quite dialogue heavy. But for the most part it feels like it's warranted as it's trying to cover the Manhattan Project, the life of Oppenheimer, and the political fallout of all this in the ensuing decades. So in IMAX the scale and detail make it easier to get through the length. But you should probably get a pitstop before you see this. This isn't a chill historical drama, this is an immersive and tiring experience that will stick with you.

Bought a Logitech M240 Silent ($24.99 at best buy, checked out Sept 2) to replace my 2 year old main mouse (MX Anywhere 3, $79.99). 3 weeks in - For most people don't spend the extra $55 

This mouse is Bluetooth only, no logi bolt reciever. It took like 4 seconds for it to connect to my M2 Mac Air. 
The scroll wheel is a basic notched type of scroll, not the free spin "hyper speed" scroll like the MX has. It does take longer to fly through a 2000 row spreadsheet. 
Has two side buttons like the MX and can easily remap them in the logi options+ app. 
The sensor is only 4000 DPI vs. 8000 with the MX anywhere 3. I never had a problem on the desk but using my lap, using my knee as a mousepad I had occasional skipping. 

M240 does have a battery life advantage. Logitech says 18 months on one AA. I've been using it a month and still 100% on the app. The MX Anywhere 3 charges with usb-c so i have to charge it every 2-3 months with normal usage. 
Also, the M240 is 15g lighter. (78 vs. 99g). That might be a big deal for some if you're lugging it to a coffee shop every day like I am. 
It does feel a little cheaper. (More "click" hollow sound, has a visible seam on the bottom) 
But the actual clicks are quieter which is nice when I'm on calls. 

If you only need to pair with 1 computer and don't really want the multi device switching. (The MX anywhere 3 supports 3 via Logi bolt or Bluetooth with button press) 
This M240 can do 90% of the daily usage for 1/3 the price. 
I'll use the MX for desk use and M240 for travel.

I just got the Logitech M240 Silent mouse ($24.99 at Best Buy, bought on 9/2) to replace my MX Anywhere 3 ($79.99) which I've been using as my primary mouse for 2 years. After 3 weeks of use, I'd say if you're an average user, don't spend the $55.

去年10月在小区下捡了个三花，取名"豆浆"，从此进入了烧钱养猫的道路。算了算一年真的花了小两万，新手避坑指南奉上！

第一坑：买猫粮乱花钱，开始听信某网红博主的"天然粮"安利，一大袋子大几百块。豆浆吃完了就稀拉拉，晋阳宠物医院去了3次，化验和打针都花了1100+。后来医生说，许多猫咪都不适合高蛋白配方的，吃个基础款处方猫粮才有用，不用迷信贵就是好

第二坑：没有提前绝育，养猫就溜达。11月底，豆浆晚上嚎叫一晚上，邻居找上门来敲门抗议，我才赶紧预约绝育，正好碰上旺季，加急多花500。没想到6个月左右就需要提前安排。

第三坑：冲动购买玩具和猫爬架。双十一晚上冲动买了近3000的猫爬架，自动喂食机，智能猫砂盆，猫砂盆老是卡纸，咸鱼上400都卖不掉，心疼！

最大一次开销是在3月份，误吞一根牙线，十点半送去宠物急诊拍片内窥镜取牙线，一共4800！吓的我当场买了680/年宠物医疗险。

其实这两万肯定是有至少一半都是交"学费"的，比如买贵的别买对的，冲动购买存货，不提前绝育、防止误食，如果你也是刚开始养猫，建议做一份靠谱的就医医院备用，提前向兽医打听基础疫苗、绝育时间安排。玩具够用就行了，别听种草文忽悠。

去年10月小区楼下捡了个三花，取名豆浆，从此踏上了烧猫钱的道路。一算账第一年确实多了小两万，写一写避避坑给新手们。

1.随便买猫粮。一开始听信某网红博主给推荐的“天然猫粮”一袋大几百，结果豆浆吃完一屁股稀了，去晋阳宠物医院看了三次，光化验打针就花了一千多。后来医生说很多猫不适合高蛋白配方的，换个普通版处方粮就活了，不要迷信贵的就是好的。

想想两万多，至少一半是“交学费”。贵的不如对的，一时兴起屯货，没提前绝育没防误食。新猫奴们建议：一份靠谱的应急医院备好。基础疫苗、绝育时间提前问兽医要。玩具能用就行，别被种草文洗脑了。

2.没有提前绝育就放出。11月底豆浆一直嚎，一晚上邻居敲门来投诉。我慌张的预约绝育。刚好医院最旺季了。多交了500的加急。后来说半年左右就要提前约时间了。

3.冲动消费。玩具猫爬架。双11一晚上疯狂下单。快3000块的猫爬架，自动喂食器，智能猫砂盆。结果猫砂盆老卡纸。闲鱼400没人要。亏的肉疼。

10月小区楼下三花寻宝，一包豆浆，从此烧钱养猫。一年下来确实多花小两万，回来仔细算算，给新手避个坑

结论：12k杭州月薪，完全可以存出第一个10万，我用了19个月（22年3月-23年10月），从0存到10.3w。

我有我的账本，清晰明确。

来分享几个步骤。

1. 知道钱花哪去了

2022年1月，我开始记账。用随手记，坚持2个月才发现，我光是外卖和奶茶就花了2800+。因为这里滨江，外卖随便一个30+。然后下午会买一杯喜茶，Manner，一个月吓人。

2. 强制储蓄。发薪日每月10号，到账立刻5000转到另一个招行卡（没绑定支付），剩下7000里，3000租房（滨康地铁站附近，跟人合租主卧独卫）。4000满足所有花费。

有人会说，5000很多。事实上，第一个月很难，但是适应后就习惯了。最关键的是，你压根碰不到这5000。

3. 伙食费是大头。自己做吧。

大概从22年4月开始，基本上都是自己做晚饭。中午带饭。周末去联华，拼多多买菜。一般食材一礼拜，150左右。然后上班日，中午在公司食堂吃。12块。

一个月伙食费压到1200内，比之前一半还要少。

社交，不是不社交。而是无效的饭局，砍掉。好朋友，在家涮个火锅也能很开心啊。

第一个10w别想搞个理财什么的赚多少了。先把这个10w攒出来。本金太小，收益率没意义。
说点真话。
存钱的难点，不是方法。而是心态。23年春节，我差点就崩了。回老家过年8000+。心痛半个月。但后来想通了。存钱，不是苦行。而是让自己有选择权。
23年10月。余额超过10w的那天。我给自己买了switch当做奖励。奖金池里，我用1500，不碰本金。
目前在冲刺第二个10w。目标25年中。
你也行。从下次发薪日开始吧。

我最后自己diy申请，并非因为中介一定不好，只是听着"保底top50"安全感十足，但问细节又很虚

去年的3月份去杭州见了一家中介，顾问(李老师)说的"你这样，英国top50保底没问题"。当时情况如下：普通一本，金融，均分86.4，雅思7.0，没有考Gmat，实习只有一个杭州券商的3个月经历。签约费2.8w，6个学校。文书单独6000

我说"保底的top50哪几个？"，给了一个名单，其中有两个确实是综合在英国top50，但是一个专业很靠后。一个需要相关工作经历。更恶心的是，顾问"文书老师深度挖掘经历"，后面我发现，朋友圈他们的文书案例，很多就是把学生名字换了，句式结构几乎一样

4月18日的一次沟通下决心diy的。中介把我的专业从"金融分析"改成了"商业管理"，理由就是好申请。我本科毕业论文是银行风控，实习还干过信用评级。更适合申请金融科技啊。这感觉就是他们为了提高下签率，而不是帮我找到最合适的那一个

所以我就自己写了个excel表，把英国32所学校的课程设置，学费，申请截止日，语言要求，往年录取情况都写上了。然后每天晚上下班后查官网。周末找学长学姐在读确认。文书没有堆砌自己从小的对金融的热爱，而是写了2022年8月份参与的企业授信项目。和如何让我想到去研究金融科技风控

最后申请了8所学校，有5个offer。爱大，曼大，华威，最后华威金融科技硕士。总花费在3000块左右。主要是申请费，材料认证，送语言

diy并不一定比中介好。要你自己承受信息获取，时间管理，结果的不确定性。但起码，每个材料都是自己负责，每个决定都有理由。保底top50就是个卖点。真实保底应该是"你知道自己的条件，你想得到啥，风险在哪，理性选择"。

我最后选择了 DIY 不是因为中介一定不靠谱，是因为保底top50听起来很稳，实际问起来非常空。

zh_zhihu_16_luna.text:
2024年4月，当我收到东京大学工学系研究生院offer之后。很多人最先反应就是：“东京一个月得两三万吧？” 但我在东京文京区本郷校区附近住了半年，每个月平均花费8000元人民币（按100日元≈4.8元计算）并没有这么夸张。

首先是房租，因为没抽中学校宿舍，我和同实验室的山田健太在千驮木合租了两室一厅。房租+管理费+水电，每个人均摊下来一个月大概4.2w日元，也就2000元人民币。房间不大只有45平米。走路到本郷三丁目站12分钟，但骑自行车到实验室8分钟。东京房租贵，主要别迷恋“离车站三分钟”。多走十分钟能省很多钱。

然后是吃饭，大概一个月2.5w日元，1200元左右。早餐一般都是超市打折面包加牛奶。午饭在学校食堂，工学部食堂套餐一般500日元。咖喱饭更便宜。晚饭一般我每周做四五次。鸡胸肉，鸡蛋，卷心菜，米饭是我的标配。晚上八点之后去本郷附近的西友打折。便当和生鱼片经常打7折。偶尔去池袋和中国同学吃火锅，一次大概3000日元。但一个月估计也不会超过2次。

我交通费控制在6000日元之内。平常都是骑自行车。只有去新宿听讲座，或者去横滨办事才会坐电车。手机套餐用日本的便宜sim卡。一个月990日元。网络室友一起用。大概一人2000日元。冬天水电煤气会涨到7000日元左右。夏天大概5000日元。

剩余的花费就是教材，咖啡，社交等。我给自己机动预算每个月1.5w日元。也就是买一两本书专业书。或者周末去上野公园，神保町逛逛。东京大学的图书馆资源非常丰富。很多资料不需要买。

当然，这个前提是：我没有买车，没有频繁旅游。没有算学费进去。如果天天出去吃。住在涩谷新宿。每周去居酒屋。8000元肯定不够。其实不是因为日本便宜。而是提前规划住的地方。自己做饭。接受普通但是方便的东京生活。研究生最贵的地方，往往不是房租，而是没有预算观念。

在2024年4月份收到东京大学工学系研究生院offer的时候，大家第一反应都是：东京一个月不得23万？但是在东京文京区本郷校区附近呆了半年的时间，一个月平均花费折合人民币8000左右（按100日元≈4.8），确实没那么离谱。

最大的支出是房租。学校宿舍抽签失败，于是同实验室山田健太一起租了个千驮木两室一厅。租金+管理费+水电分成下来，一个人每月差不多4.2万日元，合2000RMB。45平米的小房子距离本郷三丁目站走路12分钟，但自行车去实验室8分钟就能到。东京的房租的确贵，但是不要纠结“距离车站三分钟”，多花十分钟可以节省很多。

第二大支出是吃。每月约2.5万日元，合1200RMB的样子。早餐一般是超市打折面包+牛奶。午餐在学校内食堂。工学部食堂里有套餐（500日元左右），或者咖喱饭（便宜）。晚饭我一周做个四五次。鸡胸+鸡蛋+卷心菜+米饭循环。晚上八点后来到本郷附近西友，经常看到便当和生鱼片打七折的。偶尔跟中国同学去池袋吃火锅。大概3000日元一次，但不会超过一个月2次。

第三大支出是交通，控制在6000以内。平时骑自行车。只有去新宿上课（讲座），或者横滨办事坐电车。手机套餐用的是日本低价SIM卡，月租990日元。网络和室友拼着用，每人大概2000日元。冬天水电煤气会涨到7000+左右，夏天5000的样子。

剩下的就是书本，咖啡，社交啥的了。每个月会留出1.5万日元机动，买个1/2本书，或者周末去上野公园、神保町看看。东京大学的图书馆真的好，很多东西都不用买。

当然是有前提的。我没买车，没怎么旅游，学费不包括。如果每天都外食，住涩谷或者新宿，每周都居酒屋的话，8000绝对不够。不是“日本便宜”，而是早做打算住宿舍，自己做饭，并且能适应东京这种普通但是便利的生活。研究生阶段，最贵的是没有预算观念，而不是房租。
